newsitem.title: FINLAND: ICE HOCKEY-SAUNAS TOP LUXURIES AT NEW STASIUM.
newsitem.headline: ICE HOCKEY-SAUNAS TOP LUXURIES AT NEW STASIUM.

text.p: Spectators at the ice hockey world championship will be surrounded by every imaginable luxury -- and then some.
Helsinki's newly-built stadium offers much more than a chilly plastic seat and a couple of hot-dogs -- it has all any fan could wish for and even boasts two saunas overlooking the rink.

"Swedes who have seen this have said it is so typically Finnish; we just have to put saunas everywhere," Leena Itkonen, head of public relations, said before the championships gets underway on Saturday.

The stadium owners say its state-of-the art technology and services make it the most modern in the world, able to meet every possible need -- a claim thousands of fans will test at the championship which start on Saturday.
Hanging above the ice are the largest TV screens in the world -- each measuring some 30 square metres -- ready to whirl through replays and highlights.
Touch-screen Internet terminals line the hallways and the owners guarantee cellular phone connections -- a must for Finns, one-third of whom have mobile phones.
Three fully-licensed restaurants and 15 fast-food outlets, some of which sell beer, will feed and water the crowds, who will also be serviced by 415 toilets.
The saunas have one-way windows to offer total privacy to the suites which hold up to 20 people.
They cost 12,000 markka ($2,200) per night on top of the ticket and were fully booked for the championship long before the stadium was ready.
Finns take ice hockey very seriously but the 300 million markka ($60 million) stone and glass venue is more than just a sports venue.
Its main owner Harry "Hjallis" Harkimo says that is the only way to ensure it makes good money.
"Ice-hockey is the bread-and-butter of course but the profits are in all the other stuff," he said.
Owner of national champions Jokerit and known as a stubborn lone-wolf entrepreneur, Harkimo has sailed solo around the world and has transformed Jokerit this decade.

His personal persistence has been vital in getting the stadium built -- the idea initially met strong resistance among city planners and the ice-hockey jet-set, who derided it as financially shaky and over-ambitious.
Now they can watch matches from one of the 78 VIP suites or the 1,544 "priority" seats, which give access to a bar not open to ordinary fans, who take the capacity up to 13,665.

The blue seats filling the regular stands provide a fine view -- for hockey, a rock concert or whatever else comes along -- and special plastic money cards valid only in the stadium aim to limit queues at the fast-food counters.

If the brawling on the ice gets too staid or the music too loud, a video game arcade includes Wayne Gretzky 3D Hockey plus pinball machines. Customised multi-media Internet terminals also offer 60 international cable television channels.
Telecom Finland has invested heavily to make the stadium a show-room for its latest innovations and set up four mobile phone base stations so audiences can stay on-line even if the networks get busy.
"We can handle 8,000 calls simultaneously," project manager Pekka Korpimies said.
The Finnish press has highlighted poetential traffic problems -- there is parking for only 1,421 cars -- but championship organisers are happy enough.
"I don't think Hjallis wants people to come by car," said Itkonen, pointing at one of the bars. "No, we want people to stay long after the games have ended."
